title: Unveiling the Potential and Limitations of Large Observational Data Sets for the Calibration of Scaling Laws of Water Consumption
content:
Abstract

Scaling relationships for residential water consumption are crucial for transferring knowledge across spatial units and for developing predictive models that generalize beyond the observed data, key to the efficient and resilient management of urban water systems. However, calibration of their parameters is often limited by the size of the available observational data sets, which is usually small due to technological constraints, and by the violation of homogeneity assumptions underlying theoretical formulas. This research leverages a significantly large data set of observations collected at the morning peak hour in a real-world community to provide reliable estimates of scaling laws, assessing the combined impacts of the Finite Population Effect (FPE) and cross-correlation among users, and exploring the suitability of “artificial” data sets as surrogates of observations. Results show that scaling laws of variance and higher-order moments are extremely sensitive to the dependence among users and to the distribution of sample moments across the population, with impacts difficult to disentangle from finite-size sampling effects. The FPE mainly affects the estimate of uncertainty and the scaling behavior of correlation coefficients, with cascading effects on higher-order moments, whereas average correlation among users directly impacts the scaling behavior of aggregated variance. Common empirical scaling formulas are tested, highlighting important limitations in their interpretation across broad aggregation ranges. Finally, limitations are highlighted regarding the use of surrogate data sets to infer the scaling behavior of a real-world community.
